messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: School Counselor
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marisol is a 26-year-old school counselor who came to treatment describing a life organized around watching people carefully, even when she knows she is supposed to feel safe. She grew up in a small apartment with her mother and her mother’s boyfriend, and when she speaks about the violence she witnessed there as a child, the account comes in broken starts. She can begin with the hallway light, or the sound of a chair scraping, or her mother’s voice dropping suddenly quiet, but when she tries to explain the whole thing clearly she loses the thread and stops. What remains consistent is the scene itself: being a girl in that apartment, hearing an argument turn, seeing her mother cornered, and knowing before anyone said a word that something bad was about to happen. She remembers standing there and feeling that she had done something wrong simply by being present, by speaking at the wrong time, by not doing the right thing soon enough. Even now, Marisol has come to believe that the violence happened because of the way she acted, though she can move only a few sentences into the memory before emotion overtakes her and she has to look away or ask to pause.

What also stayed with her was the conviction that the adults and systems that should have protected her family did not. In her telling, there were people who knew enough to intervene and did not, and this has hardened into a broader expectation that people cannot be trusted. She notices herself scanning others almost immediately, trying to determine who is dangerous, who might turn, who is only pretending to be kind. She does this with strangers and colleagues alike, but it is especially striking at work. As a school counselor, she spends her day in offices, hallways, and conference rooms with students, teachers, and parents. In team meetings she quietly chooses the seat where her back is against the wall and her eyes can cover the room. If someone enters late and passes behind her chair, her shoulders tighten before she can think. When a distressed student reaches for her hand unexpectedly or a coworker touches her arm to get her attention, she reacts with visible alarm, a sharp intake of breath and a recoil that she later feels embarrassed trying to explain.

Her own apartment does not feel exempt from this watchfulness. Marisol said she is on guard even at home, checking where doors are, orienting herself to sounds in the building, and settling only if she can position herself so no one is behind her. She knows this makes little sense to other people, but to her body it feels necessary. The sense of danger can arrive without warning. A certain tone of voice through a wall, the sound of movement in a neighboring apartment, the abrupt shift in the atmosphere when people nearby become tense—something in her surroundings can suddenly bring back the full memory. In those moments she is not simply remembering that the violence happened; she feels flooded by it and cannot continue whatever she is doing until the wave passes.

Over the years she has also stayed away from the place where it happened. She avoids going near the old neighborhood and takes different routes to prevent accidental proximity. The avoidance is deliberate and carefully reasoned: she is certain that being there would bring everything back too strongly, and she does not trust herself to stay steady if that happened in public. At the same time, she spends long stretches thinking about how it could have been prevented. She turns over tiny details from childhood with the logic of an impossible review: if she had not spoken, if she had spoken sooner, if she had stood somewhere else, if someone had noticed more. These thoughts do not reach a conclusion, but she returns to them anyway.

What finally brought Marisol to seek help was the strain of trying to do a job centered on safety and support while feeling perpetually braced herself. She had a recent moment in her office when a parent leaned in unexpectedly to thank her and touched her shoulder; she startled so strongly that both of them froze. She went home ashamed and then angry, sitting in her apartment with her back pressed to the wall, thinking again about all the people who had failed her family and all the ways she still expects danger. She wants help because she is tired of living like this, tired of arranging every room and every encounter around the possibility of threat. What frightens her most is that she will always be this watchful and that trust, for her, may never feel possible. What she hopes for, more quietly, is to be able to remember what happened without being overwhelmed by it and to feel safe in her own home.
